topic: Understanding Distribution Channels – Concept & Progress
t: A channel in which the producer sells to a wholesaler, who sells to a retailer, who sells to the consumer is a:
e: Two intermediaries (wholesaler and retailer) stand between producer and consumer, so it is a two-level channel. A three-level channel would add a jobber or agent.

topic: Channel Mix Decisions and Distribution Strategy
t: A luxury watch maker allows only one authorised dealer in each city. This is an example of:
e: Exclusive distribution grants a single outlet territorial rights, supporting premium image and dealer commitment; selective uses a few outlets and intensive uses as many as possible.

topic: Channel Mix Decisions and Distribution Strategy
t: Which of the following is NOT a service output that customers seek from a channel, as per channel-design theory?
e: Service outputs are lot size, waiting time, spatial convenience, product variety and service backup. The producer's manufacturing cost is internal and not a customer service output.

topic: Channel Mix Decisions and Distribution Strategy
t: A new private life insurer with limited capital wants rapid nationwide reach within two years. The most appropriate channel-mix decision is to:
o: Partner with banks and other corporate agents while building agency gradually
Build a 50,000-strong tied agency force before launch
Sell only through its own branches
e: Corporate agency/bancassurance gives immediate access to an existing customer base and branch network at variable cost, suiting a capital-constrained insurer; agency takes time and fixed investment to build.

topic: Channel Mix Decisions and Distribution Strategy
t: 'Channel power' based on an intermediary's belief that the producer has special knowledge is called:
e: French and Raven's bases of power: coercive (threat), reward (benefit), legitimate (contractual right), expert (knowledge) and referent (identification). Expert power rests on perceived knowledge.

topic: Channel Mix Decisions and Distribution Strategy
t: An insurer sells the same term plan through its website at a premium 10% lower than through agents. Agents complain that customers meet them for advice and then buy online. This is an example of:
e: Conflict between different channel types serving the same market (agents versus the insurer's own online channel) is multi-channel conflict; horizontal conflict would be between two agents.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: The minimum educational qualification for appointment as an individual insurance agent under the IRDAI (Appointment of Insurance Agents) Regulations, 2016 is:
e: The 2016 regulations require the applicant to have passed at least the 10th standard (or equivalent) and to be at least 18 years of age, besides passing the prescribed examination.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: A 'Specified Person' in the context of corporate agency is:
o: An employee of the corporate agent who has passed the prescribed examination and is authorised to solicit and procure insurance business
A customer specified in the policy
e: A corporate agent solicits business only through Specified Persons who meet qualification, training and examination requirements and are registered on the IRDAI portal.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: Under the IRDAI (Insurance Brokers) Regulations, 2018, the minimum paid-up capital for a direct insurance broker is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Direct brokers need ₹75 lakh capital; reinsurance brokers ₹4 crore and composite brokers ₹5 crore. ₹25 lakh is the web-aggregator capital and ₹50 lakh is the direct broker's minimum net worth.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: A corporate agent's certificate of registration is valid for:
e: Corporate agents, brokers, web aggregators and IMFs all hold three-year registrations that must be renewed on application to IRDAI.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: Under the Brokers Regulations, 2018, the minimum paid-up capital of a composite broker is:
e: Composite brokers need ₹5 crore, reinsurance brokers ₹4 crore and direct brokers ₹75 lakh, reflecting the scale and complexity of business handled.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: A direct broker must keep a deposit with a scheduled bank of:
e: Direct brokers maintain a ₹10 lakh fixed deposit; reinsurance and composite brokers maintain 10% of their minimum capital. The deposit can be released only with IRDAI permission.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: Which of the following is a DEMERIT of the broker channel from the insurer's point of view?
o: Brokers cannot operate in more than one state
Brokers owe their duty to the client, so insurers face price competition and lower control over the relationship
Brokers cannot handle large commercial risks
Brokers are not allowed to receive remuneration
e: Because brokers represent the client and shop among insurers, insurers face pressure on price and terms and do not 'own' the customer relationship, unlike with tied agents.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: Under the bancassurance 'referral' model, the bank:
o: Owns a majority stake in the insurer
Passes customer data/leads to the insurer for a referral fee but does not solicit or sell
e: In the referral arrangement the bank only shares its customer database or refers customers; actual solicitation is by the insurer. In corporate agency the bank's Specified Persons sell the policy.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: The minimum paid-up capital required for an insurance web aggregator is:
e: Web aggregators must have ₹25 lakh paid-up equity capital and maintain net worth of at least 100% of this at all times.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: An Insurance Marketing Firm (IMF) differs from a corporate agent in that an IMF:
o: May also distribute other financial products (e.g. mutual funds, pension products) and undertake insurance servicing activities
Can tie up with only one insurer
e: IMFs solicit insurance through Insurance Sales Persons and may also market other regulated financial products and perform servicing/survey activities, subject to IRDAI conditions.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: The minimum net worth of an IMF operating in a single aspirational district is:
e: The net worth requirement is ₹10 lakh generally, relaxed to ₹5 lakh for an IMF opting to operate only in one aspirational district to encourage rural reach.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: A life insurer's 13th-month persistency ratio of 72% (by number of policies) means that:
o: 72% of claims were settled within 13 months
72% of the policies sold a year earlier were still in force after the first renewal premium fell due
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Persistency measures retention of policies at a specified duration. Low 13th-month persistency indicates mis-selling or poor need analysis at the point of sale.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: Which products may a Point of Sales Person – Life Insurance (POSP-LI) sell?
o: Pure term, non-linked non-participating endowment, immediate annuity and fixed-benefit health products
e: POS-Life products are simple, pre-underwritten products with non-medical underwriting; ULIPs and complex participating products are excluded.

topic: Distribution Channels in Insurance – Merits and Demerits
t: A micro-insurance agent under the IRDAI (Micro Insurance) Regulations, 2015 can be:
o: Only an individual who passed the agents' examination
An NGO, Self-Help Group, MFI, cooperative society, business correspondent or similar entity appointed by the insurer
e: Micro-insurance agents are entities such as NGOs, SHGs, MFIs, RRBs, cooperative banks and business correspondents that distribute micro-insurance products after insurer-provided training, without the regular agency exam.

topic: Creating Customer Value through Distribution
t: Which element forms part of 'total customer cost' in the customer-value framework?
e: Total customer cost comprises monetary, time, energy and psychic costs; product, service, personnel and image benefits make up total customer benefit.

topic: Creating Customer Value through Distribution
t: The SERVQUAL dimension 'assurance' refers to:
o: Ability to perform the promised service dependably
Knowledge and courtesy of employees and their ability to convey trust and confidence
Physical facilities and appearance of staff
e: Assurance is about competence, courtesy and credibility. Tangibles cover physical evidence, responsiveness covers promptness and reliability covers dependable performance.

topic: Creating Customer Value through Distribution
t: A customer's satisfaction after purchase is primarily determined by:
o: The commission paid to the distributor
The comparison between perceived performance and prior expectations
e: Satisfaction = perceived performance minus expectation. Over-promising at the point of sale raises expectations and leads to dissatisfaction even when service is objectively good.

topic: Creating Customer Value through Distribution
t: In the 'gaps model' of service quality, the gap between what the service provider promises in its communication and what is actually delivered is:
e: The communication gap arises when external promises exceed delivery; the knowledge gap is between customer expectation and management perception; delivery gap is between standards and actual service.

topic: Creating Customer Value through Distribution
t: A corporate agent (bank) pre-fills the proposal form from KYC records, issues the policy at the counter and sets up auto-debit of renewals. From the customer's perspective, this mainly increases value by:
o: Reducing time and energy cost and improving convenience
e: Convenience and reduced effort lower the customer's non-monetary costs, thereby raising perceived value without changing the policy benefits.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: Because insurance is intangible, distributors often use 'physical evidence' to build trust. Which of the following is physical evidence?
o: Professionally printed policy documents, branded offices and benefit illustrations
e: Physical evidence (one of the 7 Ps of services) is the tangible cues that customers use to judge an intangible service: documents, premises, staff appearance and illustrations.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: 'Moral hazard' in insurance refers to:
o: The tendency of an insured person to behave less carefully or claim more because the loss is covered
The agent's obligation to act honestly
Refusal by the insurer to pay a claim
e: Moral hazard is a change in the insured's behaviour after taking cover. Distributors contribute to control by proper risk selection and disclosure at proposal stage.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: Insurance density is defined as:
o: Premium as a percentage of GDP
Per-capita premium (total premium divided by population)
e: Density is premium per head of population, usually in US dollars; penetration is premium relative to GDP. Both are low in India relative to the world average.

topic: Best Practices in Distribution Management in Insurance
t: A customer complains that his agent promised 'guaranteed 12% returns' on a participating endowment plan. The agent's statement is:
o: A misrepresentation prohibited by the code of conduct, since bonuses are not guaranteed
Correct because endowment plans always give 12%
Allowed if the customer signs the proposal
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Agents must not make unrealistic promises or guarantee non-guaranteed benefits; benefit illustrations at prescribed rates exist precisely to prevent this.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: Which statement about lapsation in life insurance is CORRECT?
o: Early lapsation causes losses to the insurer because acquisition costs exceed first-year premium margins, and also harms the policyholder
Lapsation has no connection with distribution quality
Lapsation benefits the insurer because expenses are already recovered
Lapsation is impossible in a regular-premium policy
e: First-year acquisition costs (commission, underwriting, issue) are recovered over several years; early lapses leave them unrecovered, and the policyholder loses cover and value. Lapses are strongly linked to the sales process.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: A life insurer pays its agent ₹8,750 as first-year commission on a regular-premium policy with annual premium ₹25,000. The first-year commission rate is:
e: ₹8,750 ÷ ₹25,000 = 0.35, i.e. 35%. Since April 2023 commission rates are set by the insurer's board-approved policy within the overall expenses-of-management limit.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: 'Protection gap' in life insurance means:
o: The gap between agents' targets and achievement
The difference between premium collected and claims paid
The time between proposal and policy issue
The difference between the cover people need and the cover they actually have
e: The protection gap measures under-insurance in the population; India's large gap is a prime distribution opportunity for simple protection products.

topic: Unique Aspects of Insurance Distribution: Opportunities and Challenges
t: Which factor has MOST expanded distribution opportunities in India's rural and semi-urban markets in recent years?
o: Growth of mobile internet, digital payments (UPI) and Aadhaar-based e-KYC
Reduction in the number of insurers
e: Digital identity, mobile connectivity and low-cost payment rails have made it economical to sell and service small-ticket policies in locations that were earlier unviable for intermediaries.

topic: Customer Relationship Management through Distribution
t: 'Analytical CRM' is primarily concerned with:
o: Analysing customer data to segment customers, predict churn and identify cross-sell opportunities
e: Analytical CRM mines customer and transaction data to produce insights (segmentation, propensity, lifetime value) that operational and collaborative CRM then act upon.

topic: Customer Relationship Management through Distribution
t: An insurer's data shows that 20% of its agents bring in 80% of its premium. This observation is an application of:
e: The 80/20 (Pareto) rule suggests concentrating management attention and support on the vital few high-performing agents and the most valuable customers.

topic: Customer Relationship Management through Distribution
t: RFM analysis segments customers based on:
o: Recency, Frequency and Monetary value of transactions
e: RFM scores customers on how recently, how often and how much they buy; it is a simple, widely used analytical CRM technique to prioritise contact and offers.

topic: Claims timelines
t: Under IRDAI's 2024 norms, a surveyor must be appointed within what time of a claim intimation?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Appointment within 24 hours; survey report within 15 days; insurer's decision within 7 days of the report.

topic: Customer Relationship Management through Distribution
t: A general insurer sends motor-policy renewal reminders by SMS and WhatsApp 30 days before expiry, with a one-click payment link. This is primarily an example of CRM aimed at:
e: Renewal management is a retention activity; timely multi-channel reminders and frictionless payment reduce lapses and protect renewal income.

topic: Customer Relationship Management through Distribution
t: The 'loyalty ladder' in relationship marketing moves a customer from prospect to:
e: The ladder of loyalty (prospect → customer → client → supporter → advocate → partner) describes deepening relationship; CRM aims to move customers up the ladder.

topic: Best Practices in Distribution Management in Insurance
t: The 'fact-find' stage of the sales process involves:
o: Submitting the proposal form to the underwriter
Gathering information about the customer's income, dependants, goals, existing cover and risk appetite
e: Fact-finding precedes recommendation; it is the foundation of suitability and need-based selling and should be documented.

topic: Best Practices in Distribution Management in Insurance
t: A benefit illustration shown to a life insurance prospect must:
o: Be optional for policies above ₹10 lakh
Be prepared by the Insurance Ombudsman
Show projected benefits at the two assumed rates of return prescribed by IRDAI and be signed by the prospect and the agent
Show returns at the highest rate the agent chooses
e: IRDAI requires a standardised benefit illustration at prescribed gross investment-return assumptions so that customers are not misled by unrealistic projections; it must be signed by both parties.

topic: Best Practices in Distribution Management in Insurance
t: Which recruitment practice is MOST consistent with best practice in building a quality agency force?
o: Structured selection based on market reach, aptitude and financial stability, followed by induction training
Recruiting anyone who agrees to buy a policy themselves
Recruiting without any interview to meet headcount targets
Recruiting only relatives of existing agents
e: Quality recruitment (profiling, interviews, natural-market assessment) reduces attrition and orphan policies; recruiting for headcount alone produces low-productivity agents who exit quickly.

topic: Best Practices in Distribution Management in Insurance
t: 'Twisting' as a malpractice means:
o: Inducing a policyholder to surrender an existing policy to buy a new one, to the policyholder's detriment
e: Twisting (or churning) harms customers through surrender losses and fresh acquisition costs; it is prohibited by the agents' code of conduct.

topic: Best Practices in Distribution Management in Insurance
t: A life insurer compares channels on the ratio of policies lapsed within the first year. Agency shows 30%, bancassurance 22% and online 12%. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate?
o: Lapse rates are unrelated to channel
Point-of-sale quality in the agency channel needs attention, e.g. through better need analysis and PIVC
e: Channel-wise persistency comparisons help diagnose sales-quality problems; the remedy is improved training, suitability checks and incentive design, not blanket termination.

topic: Claims timelines
t: For health insurance, the maximum time an insurer may take to decide a cashless authorisation request under the 2024 master circular is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Cashless authorisation within 1 hour of request; final discharge authorisation within 3 hours.

topic: IRDAI Initiatives towards Expansion of Insurance Business
t: 'Bima Vahak' is an IRDAI initiative to:
o: Create a women-centric, Gram Panchayat-level field distribution force to reach rural households
e: Bima Vahak focuses on recruiting women-led distribution at the Gram Panchayat level to improve rural awareness and access, as part of the 'Bima Trinity' with Bima Sugam and Bima Vistaar.

topic: IRDAI Initiatives towards Expansion of Insurance Business
t: 'Bima Vistaar' is best described as:
o: An affordable composite product bundling life, health, personal accident and property covers for underserved segments
e: Bima Vistaar is the bundled, low-cost product designed to be sold by Bima Vahaks and through Bima Sugam to extend coverage to rural and low-income households.

topic: IRDAI Initiatives towards Expansion of Insurance Business
t: Under IRDAI's 'State Insurance Plan' / lead insurer approach:
o: Each state sets up its own insurance company
Only public-sector insurers may operate in a state
A lead insurer is designated for each state/UT to coordinate efforts to improve insurance awareness and penetration there
e: Modelled on the lead-bank scheme, a lead insurer coordinates with the state government and other insurers to drive coverage and awareness in every district and Gram Panchayat.

topic: IRDAI Initiatives towards Expansion of Insurance Business
t: The IRDAI (Expenses of Management, including Commission, of Insurers) Regulations, 2024 primarily:
o: Merged the 2023 commission and EoM regulations so that insurers fix commission under a board-approved policy within an overall EoM ceiling
Fixed agent commission at 15% for all products
e: From April 2023 individual commission caps were removed and from April 2024 a single EoM regulation governs total expenses including commission, giving insurers flexibility to pay channels differently.

topic: IRDAI Initiatives towards Expansion of Insurance Business
t: The foreign direct investment limit in Indian insurance companies was raised to 74% by the Insurance (Amendment) Act of:
e: FDI was 26% from 2000, raised to 49% in 2015 and to 74% in 2021, to bring more capital for growth and distribution expansion.
